blocks.text: About
Dor Fellous is a Tel Aviv–based multidisciplinary designer and artist working between fashion, sculpture, and material experimentation.

Drawing and sculpting were his earliest forms of expression, long before fashion entered the picture. Creating objects was a way to process intensity, to externalize emotion, to give physical presence to what could not be spoken. Sewing entered later and gradually expanded that language. Fabric became sculptural. The body became both structure and surface.

His only formal training consists of two three-month courses at Shenkar’s External Studies Department, one in sewing and one in free pattern making. Everything beyond that evolved independently, through obsessive self-learning and continuous practice.

Parallel to working with textiles, Fellous began teaching himself digital tools. Starting from 3D modeling, he moved into CLO3D, animation, augmented reality, 3D printing, and later AI-based image and concept generation. Each new medium was not a departure, but an extension, another way to test form, tension, silhouette, and movement before or beyond the physical garment.

Over the past years, he developed a personal discipline of constructing a full outfit almost every weekend. What began as garments for nightlife environments gradually became his daily wardrobe. The boundary between costume and life dissolved. Dressing became a continuous act of authorship.

His work is rooted in material exploration. Faux leather, silicone, textured synthetics, industrial hardware, mesh, Tyvek, latex, and 3D- printed components coexist within the same silhouette. He is drawn to unconventional materials, substances that resist comfort, that hold structure, that feel closer to objects than traditional garments. Many pieces exist somewhere between clothing and artifact.

Throughout this period, he produced an excessive number of works. Some endured. Others tore, collapsed, or were dismantled. The process became less about permanence and more about experimentation, testing durability, adaptability, and the emotional weight a form can carry.

Rather than operating within seasonal cycles, Fellous builds an evolving body of work shaped by repetition, nightlife, daily life, technology, and transformation, a continuous dialogue between inner states and material form.
Portfolio Approach
This portfolio is not structured as a mechanical archive of projects.
It unfolds as an ongoing journey. A visual progression shaped by moments, materials, and transformations rather than fixed seasons or categories.

The works presented here move between fashion, sculpture, digital experimentation, and wearable objects. Some are documented as finished pieces. Others appear as fragments, processes, or mutations. Together, they form a continuous narrative rather than a closed collection.

While technical explanations and process documentation are included, interpretation is intentionally left partially open. The pieces function as artworks as much as garments. They invite the viewer to observe, question, and construct meaning.
This portfolio is not meant to be consumed quickly. It is meant to be experienced.
Project “Recreate”

Recreate is an early and formative project in my practice, born out of a period of disintegration, breaking, and confrontation. It is a material and emotional research that dealt with fluidity, exposure, and an unmediated truth, one that is placed directly in front of the face.

The project was created as part of a personal journey of self recognition and confrontation with darker sides, through full surrender to pain, trauma, and unprocessed emotions. In my childhood, I was involved in a bus accident that left a significant scar on my forehead. As part of a process of aesthetic reconciliation with the scar, I worked directly with its materiality, and with organic and symbiotic materiality in general, in order to transform what is perceived as a “flaw” into a wearable aesthetic element.
Recycled silicone mesh coverings, black silicone.
A nylon coat wrapped in liquid latex to create volume and three dimensional texture.

The practice during this period was emotional and cathartic, accompanied by drawings, sculptures, and a constant stretching of material, bodily, and perceptual boundaries. As an inseparable part of my practice, I wear all of my creations myself, whether in everyday life or in nightlife contexts. Part of the progression and research lies in examining how the garment responds to movement, how it changes, wears down, erodes, and gradually acquires a more consolidated personality over time. The project also examined the response of the world: how people react to the appearance, what it activates in them, and the transformation of the flawed and the ugly into something beautiful, touching, emotionally charged, and aesthetic. Shown here was the first collection I created after completing the three- month sewing course at the External Studies Department, Shenkar College. At the time I was still in the army and living at my parents’ house, in a relatively protected and supported environment. The collection featured the use of neoprene and scuba fabrics, with a puffier and bulkier aesthetic. 2016. Re;Born Re;Create Use of silicone, latex, sculpting in liquid latex, fabrics dipped in metal coating paints that create a rigid hardened layer for structure and construction. A neck piece made of iron wires wrapped in black silicone, creating a symbiotic appearance. A conceptual video and stills project. “Distillation” of the wearable collection
Re;Escape Exhibition 2018 Exhibition - Romano House, Teder - Tel Aviv.

In 2018 I was given the opportunity to present an exhibition of all the pieces I had created. I built 3D upper torso forms with arms made of iron rods and suspended each piece in the air, allowing the texture of every work to be fully visible.

The textures ranged from asphalt like surfaces to wrinkled skin effects and the identity pattern, the shoulder cut with the zipper detail. There were combinations of hardware with a button up shirt, hardware with a latex jacket, a trash bag jacket, a jacket with neck straps, a taffeta jacket with the burned face element, a face wrapped in liquid latex to create a wet, fluid appearance. Sputnik Exhibition The Sputnik Club in Tel Aviv opened its space for exhibitions and invited me to present a collection of my works. The exhibition included paintings, sculptures, and textile pieces. It was on display for one week. NEW YORK FASHION WEEK Two looks from the collection were submitted following contact from a scout, to an international competition. I won first place and was given the opportunity to present at New York Fashion Week under Flying Solo “One to Watch,” along with three months of selling wearable pieces in a Broadway Showroom.

Materials used in the two looks: Tyvek in varying thicknesses Silicone mesh Textured hammered leather Faux leather Black silicone International Digital Fashion Week Following this, an additional opportunity emerged to present the collection through a unique platform created during the COVID period, IDFW – International Digital Fashion Week. There, the collection was presented as a serialized narrative, telling the story of an ongoing journey through the experience of the pandemic, isolation, fear, confrontation, scars, and vulnerability.

The looks were designed in response to the conditions of that period, progressing in an escalating manner, from ready to wear pieces to a final avant garde statement piece that served as the culmination of the collection: a monster.

Experimenting with New Techniques Hardware has always been part of my aesthetic language. Metal and industrial hardware elements were consistently integrated into the designs. Over the years I combined textiles with hardware and created modular looks where the hardware itself became a central feature.

There is the option to replace the screw heads to achieve different visual outcomes. Hardware has always added weight and an aggressive practicality to the pieces I created, such as the double bag, the button up shirt with screws, and the vest where none of the parts are sewn together but instead connected entirely with screws. This also includes the use of nails as a spike collar. As part of working with unconventional materials I found polymer concrete and with it I sculpted one lighter that is a totem face, one lighter that looks like a finger, and a grinder shaped like an ear with a screw assembly. There were also glasses from the collection. It was essentially an attempt to play with organic body parts in a certain way, which later connected again in further developments. For the project below, I was inspired by a jacket I saw on a homeless person, a puffy jacket where the accumulated dirt and stains created a soaked, embedded, wet and unpleasant appearance. I wanted to experiment with pigments on textile in order to recreate that same visual effect. Plaster bandages for sculpting, a silicone finish, old charger cables .
all built on a painter’s canvas base, sewn into a wearable garment.

During these years, I began working intensively as a creator, with my initial point of departure being sewing and textile. The work was based on the use of non conventional materials such as recycled plastics, garbage bags, silicones, polymers, and leather that underwent various physical manipulations. The patterns were heavy and aggressive, relying on processes of deconstruction and reassembly. The visual language was violent and avant garde, often extreme, with materials that carried a wet appearance and scarred textures.
As part of various textile experiments, I explored felting and discovered the joy of creating items through ongoing handwork, something that felt deeply therapeutic and calming.

Digital Patternmaking a party producer wanted to translate characters from his graphic work into a bodysuit. This required calculating everything in CLO in 3D, dividing the body correctly, and deconstructing the digital character so it could become an accurate model for printing the texture onto fabric. That is how the final piece was developed. Since I was a child, I have worn black and worked with this color as a raw, fundamental material for my entire aesthetic , in my clothing, in my home, and in my jewelry.

After several years of confronting myself, my pain, and my past through black as a raw material, I began to challenge myself with the next material that had always been present in my aesthetic: silver , metal ,nickel. In this collection, I worked with new materials and began using 3D printing.

The need to create complete products was always there, and during the COVID period I learned 3D modeling, animation, and 3D printing. This 3D printed neck piece was created as part of a collaboration for a Shenkar graduate project. The student chose to integrate my exploration of digital pieces and fully digital model development into her project, combining computational design with physical 3D printing. The piece was printed in PLA, a corn starch based biopolymer, and despite its scale, remained lightweight and wearable. Connecting 3d prints with textile A first attempt to create a modular sleeve that connects to all garments using Velcro at the shoulder. After many different types of sleeves, there was a desire to connect 3D printing with textile. The Hard Spine Collection Constellation of Techniques
Daily Collection and Nightlife Collection

The images present a combination of an ongoing daily collection and a nightlife focused collection. These pieces are continuously developed and often produced week by week, responding to specific events, parties, or everyday situations. The work combines different materials, prints, and the integration of textile with 3D printed elements. Wearable Collection
Over the past few years, I developed a consistent practice of constructing a full outfit almost every weekend.
The pieces were originally created for nightlife and party environments, but gradually became part of my daily wardrobe as well.
This collection documents selected works focusing on the most distinctive pieces that reflect material exploration and structural experimentation.
Throughout this period, I produced an excessive number of garments. Some endured. Others deteriorated, were altered, or disappeared.
Product Development Exhibit 1: Shoes This section includes a wide range of shoe developments and material experiments.

The developments include 3D printing, manual printing with plastic polymers, the use of bicycle inner tubes, full 3D modeling, digital concept design, and additive 3D printed components applied onto existing shoe bases.

The work ranges from early stage conceptual explorations to fully realized wearable products that I now wear in my daily life and continue to develop further. Recycled Bottle Shoe The process began with recycled plastic bottles made of PETG, which I melted and reshaped into sculptural forms and structural elements. From there, I experimented with yellowed plastics and trash bags layered over plastic casts. Symbiotic Sneakers Two additional prototypes were built using layered hot glue construction.
These pieces explored a more liquid, flowing aesthetic while remaining raw and experimental.
They functioned as sculptural studies to better understand form, balance, and practical wearability before refining the final design. Platform Shoes Prototype
The prototype began with a deconstructed shoe base. Thick cardboard tubes were added to build the exaggerated platform silhouette.

The entire structure was then wrapped tightly with layered garbage bags, creating volume, texture, and a raw industrial finish. Platform Shoe (Integrating 3D Printing) The process begins with a deconstructed platform shoe used as a base. The boot is rebuilt over it using faux leather to create a new silhouette.

The full structure is 3D scanned, refined digitally, and partially 3D printed. Printed elements are reassembled onto the shoe with visible screws and hardware, which become part of the aesthetic rather than hidden details. A platform shoe that was scanned in 3D and then modeled over. The additional structure was 3D printed in flexible TPU material, printed in layers, and assembled using screws as part of the visible hardware aesthetic. Physical TPU Print 3D modeling process Slip-on Sneaker The Slip-on sneakers began as a fully digital 3D model.

From there, the design evolved into a physical piece combining faux leather and printed TPU Fillament . An initial prototype was developed to test structure and proportion, followed by a more precise final execution.
The refined version is fully wearable and continues to be part of my daily use. Living In My Shoes Conceptual Shoe Renders and 3D Process
Exhibit 2: Bags Bags, as everyday wearable objects, became another space for me to make a statement.

I was interested in what happens while walking with the bag, how it completes the look, how it shifts posture and silhouette. But also what happens when you place it on a table and it suddenly becomes a small installation.
Each bag is designed to function daily, but also to hold presence.

I worked with different materials such as leather, 3D printed elements, and textile combinations, constantly pushing the boundary between accessory and object. The goal was always to stretch the form a little further without losing usability.

All the bags are worn in everyday life. They are used, tested, lived with. The development is ongoing and evolves according to need. Vegetable Tanned Leather Bags An attempt to mimic a spine structure by sculpting, creating a scar like aesthetic and the visual appearance of a wound or stitched scar. TPU hand bag A first attempt to create a fully complete and precise 3D model of a bag, including practical functionality. The process included a small prototype followed by a finished product. Alien bag A combination of textile and faux leather, with a bag that opens into two halves. It was developed using black TPU, and later also with a rigid PLA structure based on military soles, creating an alien aesthetic. 3D Render of each bag facePhysical printed pieces after construction Stretched Ear Bag A combination of textile and a 3D sculpted oversized ear with a stretched earlobe as part of the aesthetic. A metal ring is inserted into the stretched lobe and functions as the handle. Symbiotic Lungs Bag An organic lungs bag combining textile and 3D printing. The hardware elements are also printed. The structure includes Metal screws integrated into leather straps, combining both printed and physical hardware. The bag is double and sits on the chest like lungs, creating the appearance of bionic lungs. Organic Organ Silver Bag A bag featuring a naturally textured 3D print of an exposed alien organ, combined with textile. The hardware elements are also 3D printed as part of the overall structure. Alien Egg Clutch A small, round egg shaped bag, 3D printed with a cleaner and more symmetrical texture. It features a zipper opening and functions as a clutch rather than a shoulder bag. Sea-mbiotic Bag Every period of my life, I would sew myself a bag, constantly trying and experimenting. Before this bag was created, I was sitting in a restaurant and felt the urge to sew a piece that I could place on the table, something that would look alive, like a spine, with an organic presence.

It was also a time when, for the first time in my life, I was going to the sea a lot. There was a strong sea influence during that period. That is also where the name sea- mbiotic comes from. 3D Printed symbiotic spineInserted spine within bag pattern

Exhibit 3: Glasses Here are developments of eyewear that were first created digitally in 3D and later translated into wearable products. Some were designed as clip ons for my existing glasses, and others were developed as full standalone frames. A first attempt to translate a 3D model into functional eyewear, developed on a 3D face model with specific proportions. After printing, the prototype failed, but through this process I gained an understanding of how the structural construction needs to function in order for the glasses to be practical. There was a specific development process here, an attempt to push structural and aesthetic boundaries. One exploration involved deconstructing the frame to isolate only the nose piece, which sits inside the nose, and this later evolved into another type of eyewear. Development of glasses designed to sit on the nose without the need for traditional temples, with lenses that screw directly into the frame. The piece was created as a prototype and did not move into final production. All the glasses were 3D printed and worn in daily life and at parties as part of an ongoing testing process, allowing me to understand practicality, material behavior, and construction logic. One pair was even developed as prescription glasses, including an attempt to refine how the lenses are held and secured.
Exhibit 4: Accesories “Body Extensions” Over the years, I developed a series of accessories that I live in daily. Bracelets and rings that are not occasional pieces, but extensions of my body.

The bracelets and rings are originally hand sculpted directly on my hands using a biodegradable thermoplastic material. Each piece is formed according to the exact anatomy of my wrist, fingers, and joints. They sit precisely on the articulation points, allowing full functionality while maintaining a sculptural presence. This hand sculpted process, based on biodegradable thermoplastic, allows me to shape the material while it is warm and responsive, creating a direct dialogue between body and matter.

Conceptually, they are an evolved interpretation of old school studded bracelets. What once was a flat leather band with metal studs becomes a structural, body mapped object. Influenced by the strong attitude and expressive power of nails, which many people around me were exploring as a medium, I also designed rings that extend to the fingertip and function as artificial nails. These pieces amplify gesture and create a sharper silhouette of the hand.
The jewelry functions as part of my daily identity. I live inside these objects and continue developing them constantly.

Organic Spiked Ligther Case The Organic Spike Lighter Case started from a simple thought. A lighter is something that constantly moves between people. It passes from hand to hand, especially in social situations. That makes it more than just a tool.

I wanted to redesign this everyday object and play with how it looks and how it feels to hold. The spikes change the grip and the attitude of the object. It becomes something you notice. Something you want to pick up.

It’s fun to hand to someone. It’s fun to use. It turns a basic lighter into an accessory with presence. The piece can also be worn. It works as a pendant and can hang on a chain, shifting from functional object to wearable statement. Like many of my works, it takes something ordinary and pushes it into a more expressive, identity driven space. Commercial Pieces Commercial items such as a organic spiked lighter case and a Silver cigarette box with compartments for cigarettes were produced, photographed, and sold in a store called INN7, which carries international avant garde brands. https://www.instagram.com/inn7?igsh=M3ZzNTQzYmQ1a25o https://inn7fashion.co.il/collections/dor-fellous/women?srsltid=AfmBOoo1UL-lKo7B_xnAO3R9fij2_6CcbxhQ0Nqaw9vj94lxcRGocbuw

Creative Collaborations As part of a collaboration with the Tel Aviv–based queer line Pag , I dressed the performers in pieces from my collection, with a focus on items designed for nightlife and ritualistic contexts. The looks included silicone elements, a “Face portrait” sculpted bag made of plaster and silicone, wool/ latex masks, a sculpted leather backpack, and additional wearable pieces.

In the background, 3D animations that I created were projected on screen, echoing the material language and visual atmosphere of the collection, and transforming the performance into a total environment where body, material, and digital imagery merge into a single immersive experience. The animation projected on screen was based on an original 3D environment I created, in which I built my “night laboratory” as a digital space and rendered it with a realistic visual language. The environment reflects my physical studio and material processes, translating my hands-on experimentation into a cinematic, immersive digital setting that extends the collection beyond the body and into space. PAG - https://www.instagram.com/pagtlv?igsh=ZjM2NzEzbXNmd2J0 The digital project was released and sold during the early period of the NFT movement, marking an initial exploration of distributing fashion-driven digital environments as collectible works, and extending the collection into the realm of digital ownership and virtual exhibition. https://www.nastymagazine.com/fashion/lukewarm-by-carlos-victimo/ Victimo Studio - https://www.instagram.com/carlosvictimo?igsh=MTk2dXUwcjI5N3ZscQ== Model - Tamar Alma - https://www.instagram.com/tamarialma?igsh=ZThpaGp4bmFqazkw Multiple pieces of mine were photographed in a shoot with Italian photographer Carlos Victimo from Victimo Studio, alongside additional pieces from the collection. The images were published in Nasty Magazine. The Ellesse Launch Competition
Ellesse, a well known mainstream sportswear brand, entered the Israeli market and initiated a launch competition as part of its local introduction.

A selected group of designers was invited to participate under the framework of Beit Ha’bad in Tel Aviv, a sewing and textile center. We were given full boxes of unreleased sample garments that had never reached production. The brief was to deconstruct the pieces and create a new full look that could fit within a sports related lifestyle context, whether tennis, skiing, or other athletic environments.

Over a defined period, each designer developed one complete look. The winner would have their design produced and receive the opportunity to travel to the company’s headquarters in London. and immersive presentation tools. My approach was to stay true to my design language while intentionally moving toward a more commercial direction. I focused on functionality. The garment was modular, with detachable sleeves and the ability to separate the upper and lower sections. The piece could be adapted and reconfigured according to need.
For the runway presentation, I expanded the look with 3D printed jewelry, eyewear, label tags and boot covers, integrating my sculptural language into the sportswear framework.

For the initial concept presentation, I introduced the design using augmented reality. Through an iPad, I presented the full 3D model in the room, allowing the team to walk around it and examine the details before physical production. The workflow combined CLO3D, Blender, and Adobe Aero to create the AR experience.

Although I did not win the competition, the project marked a significant exploration of merging commercial sportswear with modular construction, digital prototyping, Interview - https://www.instagram.com/p/CftjuENIIbi/?igsh=MWxud2p5cXBxbWcxMg== Beit Ha’bad - FabHouseTlv - https://www.instagram.com/fabhouse.tlv?igsh=MTlpemgzanA0a2dsdA== ELLESSE - https://www.instagram.com/ellesse_il?igsh=d2xybGgxb3l1M29k

https://www.instagram.com/ellesse?igsh=MWVoa2RzY2Vhd3c4dw== Static Although the design did not win the competition, only a few months later I was contacted by the stylist of Static, a well known Israeli singer and performer.
At the time, he was launching his new solo album, and the first music video of the project required a distinctive look. The stylist chose my modular sportswear design for the video.
I brought the more commercial version of the garment and tailored it specifically to his body and performance needs. The fit and proportions were adjusted to match his movement and stage presence.

We also incorporated my personal 3D printed jewelry into the look, expanding the visual identity beyond the garment itself. Music Video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gnJZxZfNJcw Static - https://www.instagram.com/static?igsh=MTNnaTlmeTV1OGh4ag== yes. A national television company in Israel commissioned me to create an organic shield as part of a Purim costume for reservist soldiers who had returned from the war. They provided a reference, and I was responsible for developing the model, adjusting it to be practical and dimensionally accurate, sewing the capes, and assembling the full look. Customized Headphones As part of my work with The nightlife, two DJs contacted me wanting personalized headphone pieces. At first the idea was to create some kind of Cover like structure, but later I proposed replacing the entire headband structure of the headphones and fully 3D printing it. This required building a practical model from scratch, including a ratchet mechanism so the headphones could sit properly without damaging the original form. I designed each piece according to the specific identity of the DJ. The pieces were 3D printed. I scanned the DJs in 3D to achieve accurate proportions, and then built the models accordingly. Molly Lolen, a German Israeli DJ, wanted a more organic, silver aesthetic that feels very current and trendy.

Bobaz Lobster, a local Israeli DJ, wanted a design aligned with her persona, Lobster. Molly Lollen - https://www.instagram.com/molly.lollen?igsh=MXhodnF2MzUxZ2lpMA== Bobaz Lobster - https://www.instagram.com/bobaz.lobster?igsh=NnoxanIyZjNyMThx Bruised Skin Collection As part of an attempt to revisit, after many years, the subject of scars and my personal childhood experiences, I felt a sudden desire to work with skin tones, wounded and veiny textures, like a fresh scar.

The first project was created in CLO as a 3D garment pattern featuring an extended alien like tail, with a highly organic and skin like appearance. I created a full jewelry collection based on digital concepts I had previously developed in 3D. This collection was worn by Yulia Plotkin as part of a music video shoot for a German band. The production used the first robotic camera in Israel, and the collection was featured in that project. https://youtu.be/i24Fuk74vbo?si=fC7DO5qMCGcSpnI2 Friends & Lifestyle As part of an ongoing creative phase, there was a period when friends would come to me before parties and I would assemble and build their looks from scratch.

This is one of the most iconic looks I created. It was worn by someone who worked as a selector at parties, dressed in a full, highly exaggerated look. It became a statement at the entrance, a powerful visual moment in a space where thousands of people were passing through. TOMER ROMN - 3D Face Scanning This Project began through a collaboration with Tomer Romn, a well known performer and drag artist in Tel Aviv.

As a signature gesture, Tomer used to spray paint directly onto his head, creating a kind of sculptural wig that felt like an extension of his body. He worked with different colors, turning the sprayed surface into an identity marker.

As part of a collaboration with “Beatfoot” and the creation of a song produced especially for Tomer and presented in Berlin, we decided to translate this sprayed gesture into a fully realized 3D printed piece. The goal was to give physical, dimensional form to the idea of the sprayed head. Tomer Romn Instagram :https://www.instagram.com/tomeromn?igsh=d3E3anJmNmZqbjl4 The process began with a full 3D scan of Tomer’s head. From there, I digitally modeled a sculptural piece that sits precisely on his specific head shape, following its contours exactly.
The print took 26 hours to complete.

In addition, a full look was developed using liquid metal fabric, silicone organza, and raw textile elements, constructed to sit precisely on his body. The garments were modeled digitally to align with his proportions.
Additional 3D printed Tyvek faces were created and attached to the shoes, extending the concept further into the silhouette.

Nona Chalant - Performance and Expression Nona chalant is a well known performative drag figure in Israel for the past 15 to 20 years. Our connection began following a 3D project created for Offer Nissim, where I worked as a VJ.
Over time, a deep creative bond formed between us and we began collaborating. I designed looks for productions and visual graphics for parties, and later created a look for Fashion Week.
It became a mutual creative expression, combining my tools and sculptural language with her performative power and presence.

Digital Fashion Week Following this, an additional opportunity emerged to present the collection through a unique platform created during the COVID period, IDFW – International Digital Fashion Week. There, the collection was presented as a serialized narrative, telling the story of an ongoing journey through the experience of the pandemic, isolation, fear, confrontation, scars, and vulnerability.

The looks were designed in response to the conditions of that period, progressing in an escalating manner, from ready to wear pieces to a final avant garde statement piece that served as the culmination of the collection: a monster.

Exhibit 4: Accesories “Body Extensions” Over the years, I developed a series of accessories that I live in daily. Bracelets and rings that are not occasional pieces, but extensions of my body.

The bracelets and rings are originally hand sculpted directly on my hands using a biodegradable thermoplastic material. Each piece is formed according to the exact anatomy of my wrist, fingers, and joints. They sit precisely on the articulation points, allowing full functionality while maintaining a sculptural presence. This hand sculpted process, based on biodegradable thermoplastic, allows me to shape the material while it is warm and responsive, creating a direct dialogue between body and matter.

Conceptually, they are an evolved interpretation of old school studded bracelets. What once was a flat leather band with metal studs becomes a structural, body mapped object. Influenced by the strong attitude and expressive power of nails, which many people around me were exploring as a medium, I also designed rings that extend to the fingertip and function as artificial nails. These pieces amplify gesture and create a sharper silhouette of the hand.

The jewelry functions as part of my daily identity. I live inside these objects and continue developing them constantly. AI as a Creative Tool 3D Modeling and AI Finishing

Instead of rendering traditionally, I developed a workflow where I model in 3D and use an AI engine for material rendering and finishing. This approach allows me to avoid heavy computer based rendering processes while achieving more realistic material results through AI.
It enables me to create one of a kind or on demand products intended for 3D printing. Conceptually, it allows for precise visual evaluation before printing and before wasting materials.

These are a series of tests exploring that workflow. A mini AI based collection built on recent sketches and previous works developed in Clo3d. The process became a way to relearn finishing techniques and focus on details, refining control over aesthetic nuances.

It functioned as a more study driven workflow, but ultimately brought me to a point where I can now express myself and create designs in a more fluid and accessible way. HOST Wearable Sketches. Adaptive Identities. HOST began as a shift in process. After years of working intuitively, sculpting directly in material, reacting and building through instinct, I stopped.
I sat down and started sketching deliberately. This act of drawing before making opened a new mental space.
Instead of discovering the form through matter, I began discovering it through vision.
HOST is built on that transition. The collection explores a new sketching technique powered by AI, allowing rapid visual prototyping
until a fully resolved visual product emerges.
From there, I translate the image into physical reality.

AI becomes a drafting table, not a replacement for craftsmanship. Color plays a new role here. Where I once focused on black as a single field with infinite textures, HOST introduces raw, natural, almost primitive tones:
deep blue, blood red, burnt orange, metallic silver light.

Each look often carries one dominant color, layered with material tension and surface variation. The challenge remains the same. One color. Infinite texture. Concept HOST refers to the body as a host to emotion, environment, memory, and external pressure. Every morning is a subtle act of adaptation.
The body negotiates reality. The garments reflect this negotiation. Silhouettes expand or compress the body.
Proportions shift, elongated torsos, exaggerated volumes, protective shells, organic extensions.
Some elements feel like growths.
Others feel like armor. Textures and materials change according to mood. Rigid constructions impose structure. Soft distortions absorb impact.
Surfaces resemble skin, membrane, bone, or synthetic tissue. HOST is conceptual yet translatable.
It exists as imagery, editorial storytelling, and wearable possibility. Each look represents a visual state of adaptation.
